title: Time to iron out details for how to allow EV charging across footpaths, councillors agree

Dublin City Councillors on Monday backed a motion calling for a clear process to let residents install electric-vehicle charging connections across footpaths ahead of national legislation intended to enable the practice.

The government’s 2025 draft Private Wires Bill calls for the loosening of ESB Networks’ traditional grip on electricity lines.

“Private lines will be allowed where they are the solution to allow on-street charging of electric vehicles,” says a summary of the draft bill, on the Department of Environment’s website.

But before that comes about, said Fianna Fáil Councillor Rory Hogan, who tabled the motion, the council has some work to do.

His proposal addresses a practical obstacle for people in terraced homes and apartments who lack driveways or private parking.

Residents may be willing to buy an electric vehicle and pay for a home charger, he said, but cannot easily connect it to a car parked on the public road.

As part of the effort to shift people away from burning fossil fuels – to help blunt the impacts of climate change, and reduce air pollution – the government is pushing for 30 percent of private cars to be electric vehicles by 2030.

All those EVs will need to be charged somewhere, so Dublin City Council's development plan says all new developments must include charging points. And the four Dublin local authorities together brought in a regional strategy for installing a constellation of public charging hubs.

But public charging hubs are less convenient, and the electricity they provide can be much more costly – so, many EV owners want to charge their cars at their homes. For people with driveways, that's no problem, but those without them have been searching for solutions.

That's led to the installation of charging arms that carry a power cable from a house up over the footpath to the road (the council says this is a no-no), and the installation of chargers at the road-edge of the footpath (council says nope).

Now it looks like the government and the council are moving ahead with a plan to allow residents to run wires under the footpath.

But Hogan said there are two main barriers involved in this: legislation, and the road-opening licence needed to dig up a footpath, lay the wire underneath, and then close up the trench.

He argued that the council should prepare its approach before the private wires legislation is enacted, so residents can understand how to apply, and work can be carried out safely.

“What we need is [to] figure out a way that allows residents to apply for road opening licenses to dig up the footpaths and to trench the wire in a safe and orderly manner,” he said.

“What this motion is basically trying to do is trying to make it as accessible as possible for residents to apply for road opening licenses and to install chargers outside their homes.”

“I think we need to do everything that we can to enable residents to charge their cars inside their homes,” Hogan told councillors.

At the meeting on Monday, Fine Gael Councillor Ray McAdam said the city’s infrastructure must reflect how people live, particularly in older parts of Dublin where many homes have no driveways.

While there are national targets for moving people to EVs, if the city is “serious about achieving those targets, then the infrastructure has to work for people in the real world", he said.
